sentence: A 32-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department due to a recent decrease in vision in the RE, coinciding with the appearance of a brownish lesion in that eye.
His ophthalmological history included penetrating trauma to the RE three years before he was sutured in our center.
On examination he had visual acuity of 0.1, which improved to 0.5 with pinhole vision.

Biomicroscopy of the anterior segment shows an iris cyst that occupies half of the anterior chamber, whose anterior wall contacts the corneal endothelium, a 6 mm linear corneal scar that respects the visual axis, and a transparent lens.
Intraocular pressure (IOP) is 14 mmHg in both eyes.
The fundus of the eye as far as the lesion can be explored is normal, as is the B-mode ocular ultrasound of the posterior segment.
The image obtained using Stratus OCT shows a thin anterior wall in discontinuous contact with the corneal endothelium and clear contents of the cyst.
The lesion was clinically diagnosed as an iris epithelial cyst.

The patient underwent surgery by puncture aspiration of the cyst with a 30g needle, viscodissection of the cyst to separate it from the corneal endothelium and reform of the anterior chamber followed by ab external photocoagulation in the same surgical procedure of its collapsed walls using non-confluent, high-power impacts. and long time, until tissue retraction is observed.
No intense burns were performed nor was confluent treatment applied to avoid extensive atrophy of the underlying iris.

The postoperative period was characterized by moderate intraocular inflammation that responded to hourly topical corticosteroids and the formation of a large posterior synechiae at 12 hours without developing a cataract and with significant visual improvement.
Six months after the intervention, visual acuity is 0.8 and the biomicroscopic examination shows a vertically oval pupil with posterior synechiae from X to II h as the only sequelae.
There are no signs of lesion recurrence.
